Chapter 6: The Waiting Game—Limbo, Bureaucracy, and the Quiet Toll of Uncertainty.
There’s a certain kind of exhaustion that doesn’t come from running or working hard, but from waiting.
You know that feeling? The fatigue that sets in when your life is on pause—when you wake up not knowing if you’ll be allowed to stay, or if you’ll have to start all over again tomorrow.
For people seeking asylum, the world shrinks down to a handful of offices, crowded waiting rooms, and endless lines. Every one of them is a reminder that your future rests in someone else’s hands.
For our boy—now a teenager—the journey starts to slow down. That frantic rush to escape is replaced by the slow, grinding pace of paperwork and interviews.
He finds himself sitting in rooms packed with others just like him—their faces carrying the same mix of hope and exhaustion.
Behind the desk, the officials barely look up. Their questions are short and to the point. Where are you from? Why did you leave? Do you have proof?
He does his best to answer, but how do you sum up a life in a few words? The truth is never easy to explain, and the past can feel like a puzzle with missing pieces.
Days blur into weeks, and weeks into months. The boy ends up in a shelter, sharing space with strangers—each one carrying their own story of loss and longing.
Some people get angry quickly. Others just go quiet. The boy learns to keep his head down, to avoid trouble, and to wait for news that never seems to arrive.
That constant uncertainty? It eats away at him. Makes it tough to sleep, to eat, even to hope.
Still, even in all that waiting, little routines start to form. He helps clean up around the shelter, picks up a few words of the local language, tries to keep his mind busy.
Sometimes he just watches life outside the window—people going about their day, totally unaware of the invisible lines that keep some people in and others out. Most folks never notice the waiting, or the quiet desperation of those trapped in the system.
Every now and then, there’s a glimmer of hope. Maybe a letter arrives, or an interview gets scheduled, or a caseworker offers a smile and a kind word.
Each small step forward feels like a lifeline—just enough to keep going.
But setbacks? They’re pretty common. The boy learns not to get his hopes up too high. The process is slow, unpredictable, and sometimes, it just feels unfair.
And yet, in this long stretch of limbo, the boy finds a different kind of strength. It’s not the fierce, fiery determination that got him out of danger. It’s quieter—a steady resilience. The ability to endure, to keep believing in a future he can’t quite touch yet.
Some people lose hope here, but the boy hangs on, drawing courage from memories of his mother and the dream of a better life.
Most of us never have to wait for permission to belong, to be seen, or even to exist.
For those caught in this waiting game, though, every single day is a test—a test of patience, of faith, and of finding meaning right in the heart of uncertainty.
